title: How Playing a Tree Scientist Made Tony Leung See Plants as 'Sentient Beings'
summary: Tony Leung has built a career on quiet intensity, but his latest role brought an unexpected revelation: trees might be more like us than we think. In Ildikó Enyedi's mystical drama "Silent Friend," Leung plays Dr. Tony Wong, a neuroscientist stranded in Marburg, Germany, during the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic. His research subject? The electromagnetic impulses of a ginkgo tree. The film is a triptych weaving together three stories across time, all connected to the same tree. Léa Seydoux appears as a botanist, Luna Welder as a 1908 feminist scientist, and a pair of college students experience first love in 1972. Leung's storyline anchors the present-day thread, exploring how lockdown blurred the boundaries between human and natural worlds. To prepare, the "In the Mood for Love" star dove into books on plant intelligence and early cognitive development. "It really changed my perspective toward plants," Leung said. "I see them as sentient beings, same like me, same like human beings." The shift was profound: if you respect plants, he reasoned, what about all other living beings? Enyedi, an Oscar nominee for "On Body and Soul," said she chose the 2020 setting because it was a moment when "time becomes fluid" and humanity's relationship with nature was up for reexamination. Leung, who rarely works outside Asia, said he was drawn by Enyedi's vision. "The director is the most important person, not the script," he noted. "Silent Friend" premiered in competition at Venice and is now in select theaters. For Leung, the role was more than a performance — it was a philosophical awakening. Next time you pass a ginkgo, you might just wonder what it's feeling.
why_it_matters: This story matters because it taps into a growing question for your generation: how should humans relate to nature? If even a celebrated actor can radically rethink the inner life of a tree, it forces us to consider whether our environmental choices need a deeper ethical shake-up.

background_read: Tony Leung Chiu-wai is a Hong Kong actor famous for his collaborations with director Wong Kar-wai in films like 'In the Mood for Love' (2000) and for his role in Marvel's 'Shang-Chi'. He rarely works outside Asia, making 'Silent Friend' a significant international project.

The ginkgo tree is a 'living fossil' that has remained almost unchanged for over 200 million years and is often studied for its resilience. Recent scientific research into 'plant neurobiology' explores whether plants can learn, remember, or communicate through electrical signals.

Ildikó Enyedi is a Hungarian filmmaker whose movie 'On Body and Soul' (2017) was nominated for the Academy Award for Best International Feature Film. The COVID-19 setting in 'Silent Friend' captures a time when many people felt a blur between indoor, human worlds and the natural outside.
Léa Seydoux is a French actress known for 'Blue Is the Warmest Color' and the James Bond films, while Luna Welder is a younger German actress who portrays a 1908 feminist scientist.
The Venice Film Festival is the world's oldest film festival, and premiering in competition there is a major honour that often leads to awards buzz.

perspectives.description: Leung's awakening promotes empathy for all living things, which could encourage conservation and a more careful coexistence with nature. If people see trees as sentient, they may protest deforestation and support green policies more passionately.

Many biologists warn against anthropomorphism — projecting human feelings onto plants. Critics say calling a plant 'sentient' oversimplifies science and could distract from real conservation issues by focusing on poetic metaphors rather than measurable ecosystems.

The film reflects a historical pattern: during lockdowns, many people reconnected with nature and questioned industrial growth. Examining plant intelligence through an art-house film opens a conversation that sits between hard science and philosophical wonder, mirroring debates that date back to Charles Darwin.

As climate anxiety rises, works like 'Silent Friend' could shape a cultural shift away from seeing nature as a mere resource. This may influence future school curricula to include plant ethics, or inspire young filmmakers to tackle environmental themes through personal storytelling.
